extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals / publicists pitching investigative reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for PR representatives on how to craft outreach and build relationships specifically to attract investigative reporters and supply them with usable leads or 'seeds' rather than routine press announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand what investigative reporting really is and whether it's appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative reporting is “systematic, in-depth, and original research and reporting, often involving the unearthing of secrets.” Ensure your pitch fits that remit before reaching out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pitch routine or celebratory items (e.g., funding rounds, product releases, acquisitions) to investigative reporters unless there is a scoop or hidden angle. Investigative reporters pursue deeper issues, scandals, or significant impacts; your pitch needs unique insights, exclusive “never before shared” information, or a hidden angle that aligns with investigative work. Be aware that investigative stories rely on relationships and trust—consistent outreach with tips about things that are wrong is more valuable than one-off promotional messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build and nurture deeper relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Relationships with investigative reporters require a higher level of trust and credibility than typical media relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid impersonal quick texts or mass emails; invest time to find, build, and nurture relationships. Be a reliable, substantive source who can provide credible information that could lead to impactful stories. Consistent, trustworthy interactions increase the chance reporters will act on your tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put yourself out there: research, meet, and network
rubrics_metrics.description: Know who the investigative reporters in your marketplace are and proactively introduce yourself and your capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research local investigative reporters, ask them for coffee, and be prepared with pertinent information (e.g., “here’s what I do, here are the clients I work with, if you need an expert, here are expert clients I have”). Attend public events where 'movers and shakers' gather so reporters see you in the community. Personal outreach and in-person introductions foster credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help reporters by providing substantive, actionable information
rubrics_metrics.description: Make an investigative reporter’s job easier by supplying concrete answers, proof paths, and leads they can follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pitching, anticipate and answer investigative questions such as: What happened here, and why? How much of this story is black and white? How much is a gray area? How much can I prove, and how can I prove it? How much can I “shake the trees” to get more information? What does accountability look like here? Use these as thought-starters when preparing a pitch; supply documents, data, expert names, and verifiable facts where possible to increase utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch seeds (tips), not finished stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative reporting often unfolds over time; an initial tip or hypothesis can be the start of a larger investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You do not always need a fully fleshed-out narrative—reaching out with a credible tip, lead, or seed can prompt an investigative reporter to dig deeper. Frame your outreach as a potential starting point rather than a finished feature, and be honest about what you know versus what you suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ill-timed or irrelevant pitches (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrelevant or poorly-timed pitches will be ignored and can harm your relationship with investigative reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of anti-patterns: pitching seasonal fluff (e.g., New Year's workout stories) or press-release style promotional content to investigative reporters. Such pitches are likely to be deleted or sent to the junk folder—focus on substantive, timely, and investigable matters instead.
